title: Practice: real-life graphs
intro: Nine questions, including three where you click straight on a distance–time graph, and a timed speed drill.

questions.prompt: This is a distance–time graph for a journey. **Click the section where the speed is greatest.**
hints: Greater speed means a steeper line.
Which of the three sections climbs most sharply?
questions.explanation: The first section is the steepest, so it has the greatest speed: 40 km in 1 hour, which is 40 km/h.

questions.prompt: On the same graph, **click the section where the object is not moving.**
hints: If the distance is not changing, the object has stopped.
questions.explanation: The flat middle section is where the distance stays at 40 km, so the object is **stationary**. Careful — a flat line on a *speed*–time graph would mean the opposite: moving steadily.

questions.prompt: A car travels 40 km in the first hour of its journey. What is its speed, in km/h?
questions.explanation: $\frac{40 \text{ km}}{1 \text{ h}} = 40$ km/h. On the graph this is simply the gradient of that section.

questions.prompt: On a **speed**–time graph, what does a horizontal (flat) line mean?

options.text: The object is moving at a constant speed

hints: Read the vertical axis: it is **speed**, not distance.
If speed is not changing, what is the object doing?
questions.explanation: On a speed–time graph the vertical axis is speed, so a flat line means the speed is not changing — a **constant speed**. On a *distance*–time graph the same shape would mean stationary. Always check the axis label first.

questions.prompt: Find an average speed for a whole journey.
questions.scenario: A cyclist rides 40 km in 1 hour, rests for 1.5 hours, then rides a further 15 km in 2.5 hours.

steps.prompt: What is the total distance travelled, in km?
What is the total time taken, in hours? (Do not forget the rest.)
steps.hint: The clock keeps running while the cyclist rests.

steps.prompt: Now find the average speed, in km/h.

hints: Average speed $=$ total distance $\div$ total time.
questions.explanation: $\frac{55 \text{ km}}{5 \text{ h}} = 11$ km/h. Note this is **not** the average of the two riding speeds (40 km/h and 6 km/h) — the rest and the unequal durations both pull it down.

questions.prompt: A car slows from $25$ m/s to $0$ m/s over 12 seconds. Find the size of its deceleration, in $\text{m/s}^2$. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
hints: The change in speed is $25$ m/s; divide by 12.
questions.explanation: $\frac{25}{12} = 2.083\dots \approx 2.1\ \text{m/s}^2$. As an acceleration it would be written $-2.1\ \text{m/s}^2$, but the *size* of the deceleration is $2.1$.

questions.prompt: Match each pair of axes to what its gradient measures.
hints: The gradient is always “vertical axis per horizontal axis”.
questions.explanation: A gradient is always *how much the vertical quantity changes per unit of the horizontal one*. Distance per time is speed; speed per time is acceleration; cost per item is the price; volume per time is a flow rate.

questions.prompt: **Driving at 60 km/h for 1 hour and then 20 km/h for 3 hours gives an average speed of 40 km/h.**
hints: Work out the total distance and the total time properly.
questions.explanation: False. Total distance $= 60 + 60 = 120$ km, total time $= 4$ hours, so the average speed is $\frac{120}{4} = 30$ km/h. Averaging 60 and 20 ignores the fact that far more time was spent at the slower speed.

questions.prompt: Quick-fire: speed, distance and time. Give numbers only.

pool.prompt: 120 km in 2 hours. Speed in km/h?
150 km in 3 hours. Speed in km/h?
60 km/h for 4 hours. Distance in km?
80 km at 40 km/h. Time in hours?
100 m in 20 s. Speed in m/s?
45 km in 30 minutes. Speed in km/h?
12 m/s for 30 s. Distance in m?
200 km at 50 km/h. Time in hours?
Speed goes 0 to 20 m/s in 5 s. Acceleration in m/s²?
Speed goes 30 to 10 m/s in 4 s. Size of deceleration in m/s²?
90 km in 1.5 hours. Speed in km/h?
25 m/s for 8 s. Distance in m?

questions.explanation: Everything here is one of $\text{speed} = \frac{d}{t}$, $d = s \times t$, or $t = \frac{d}{s}$. Watch the units — 30 minutes is 0.5 hours, which is why 45 km in half an hour is 90 km/h.
